walkthroughs.h2: Electrophilic addition of HBr to propene
walkthroughs.body_html:
Pi electrons of C=C attack H-Br: H added, Br- formed. Carbocation forms on either C; Markovnikov favours more stable 2° cation.

Br- attacks the carbocation -> 2-bromopropane (major). Minor product: 1-bromopropane via 1° cation.

SN1: 2 steps via carbocation; 1st order; favoured by 3° R-X, polar protic solvent. Racemic product possible.

SN2: 1 step concerted; 2nd order; favoured by 1° R-X, polar aprotic solvent. Inversion of configuration.

Haloalkane + ethanolic KOH (heat) -> alkene (elimination). Aqueous KOH -> alcohol (substitution).

Higher temperature and bulkier base favour elimination. Zaitsev's rule: most substituted (stable) alkene predominates.

mcqs.q: Why do tertiary halogenoalkanes typically react via SN1 rather than SN2?
options: Br always adds to the end carbon because it's the most accessible.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN2 because they have more bonds to break.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN1 because they are more reactive in every way.
The tertiary carbocation intermediate is stabilised by three alkyl groups (positive inductive effect), making the SN1 pathway favourable.

mcqs.q: Why does benzene undergo electrophilic SUBSTITUTION but alkenes undergo electrophilic ADDITION?
options: Benzene reacts the same way as alkenes — by addition across one of its double bonds.
Benzene cannot react with electrophiles at all.
Br always adds to the end carbon because it's the most accessible.
Substitution preserves benzene's stable delocalised pi system; addition would destroy aromaticity at a large energetic cost.

mcqs.q: When HBr adds to propene, why does Br preferentially attach to the middle carbon?
options: The more stable secondary carbocation forms preferentially as the intermediate, so Br adds there (Markovnikov's rule).
Benzene cannot react with electrophiles at all.
Br adds to whichever carbon has more hydrogens already.
Br always adds to the end carbon because it's the most accessible.
